subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Dread Risk vs. Statistical Risk
description: A quick, practical guide to Dread Risk vs. Statistical Risk.

hook.text: After a shark attack at one beach, tourism drops across the entire coast. One event, statewide fear.

buildup.text: Dread risk: catastrophic, uncontrollable events trigger outsized fear regardless of actual probability.

discovery.text: We fear plane crashes more than car crashes because dying in a plane feels uncontrollable and dramatic.

twist.text: Voluntary risks feel less scary. Skiing off-piste feels fun; a chemical plant nearby feels terrifying.

climax.text: Control, choice, and drama shape perceived risk. Statistics alone never calm dread-based fear.

quiz.question: What type of risks trigger dread?
options: Only risks with high statistical probability

details.summary: Dread risk describes the outsized fear people feel toward catastrophic, uncontrollable, and unfamiliar hazards compared to statistically larger risks that feel voluntary and familiar. People dread nuclear accidents and terrorism far more than car crashes or smoking.
details.whyItMatters: The gap between dread risk and statistical risk drives misallocation of safety resources, disproportionate regulation, and public policy that addresses fear rather than actual harm.
takeaways: Involuntary and catastrophic risks produce dread disproportionate to probability
Familiar and voluntary risks feel less threatening even when statistically larger
Public policy often reflects dread perception rather than objective risk analysis

faq.question: Why do people fear terrorism more than car accidents?
faq.answer: Terrorism scores high on every dread dimension: it is involuntary, uncontrollable, unfamiliar, catastrophic, and inequitably distributed. Car accidents are voluntary, familiar, and feel controllable. The brain weights dread factors heavily in risk evaluation.

faq.question: Should policy ignore dread risk in favor of statistical risk?
faq.answer: Not entirely. Dread reflects real values beyond probability, including equity, control, and catastrophic potential. But policy should be transparent about the gap between perceived and statistical risk so resources are allocated with awareness of both dimensions.
